issues.issue: The Schedule of Named Insureds lists only "Farm Nutrients LLC", while the endorsement header and Item 1. name Rembrandt Enterprises, Inc. as the insured. Whether Rembrandt is itself a "named insured" — a status that matters under II.A., V.S. and IX.G. — is not resolved by the schedule.

The additional insured is covered "solely with respect to their vicarious liability arising out of any 'named insured's' direct liability", a formula that does not say what happens where the additional insured is alleged to be directly at fault alongside a named insured. "Vicarious liability" is undefined and does the whole work of the grant.

The grant covers business interruption loss "during a 'period of interruption' in excess of the Deductible Period", comparing a loss amount with a period of time; whether the Deductible Period bars the first three days' loss or defers coverage entirely is not stated here. The mismatch of measures makes the trigger unclear.

The condition requires the loss to be reported "during the 'policy period'" although Condition IV.B. lets the period of interruption run until operations could reasonably be restored, potentially after expiry. A loss not yet incurred by expiry cannot be reported within the period the condition demands.

The $5,000,000 sublimit is made "subject to the Limits of Liability identified in the Declarations", but those limits (Items 2., 3. and 4.) are expressed in Section II. as caps on "claims", "remediation costs" and "legal defense expense" — not on business interruption loss. How the sublimit erodes or is capped by the Declarations limits is unresolved.

The clause excludes loss "incurred during the Deductible Period" without saying when that three-day period begins — at the pollution condition, at discovery, or at suspension of operations. The start date is left indeterminate.

"Business income" mixes net profit "that would have been realized had there been no 'business interruption'" with continuing operating and payroll expense, excluding certain payroll, and with temporary rent. Whether continuing expenses are recoverable in addition to, or only within, the hypothetical profit figure is not stated.

"Business interruption" requires a "necessary partial or complete suspension" of operations, with no measure of what makes a suspension necessary or how partial a slowdown must be to count. Both qualifiers are without boundary.

"Covered pollution condition" exists only where remediation costs from first-party discovery are covered under Coverage A. or B., so Endorsement 12's Fungi and Legionella exclusion and Exclusion VI.N. (Naturally Occurring Materials) may remove the predicate entirely. Whether any business interruption coverage survives those exclusions is a whole-instrument question.

"Delay expense" applies only "for a 'covered location' under development" — a phrase never defined — and its enumerated list of additional costs (with one item left unnumbered) admits no comparable expenses. The scope of the enumerated list against unlisted delay costs is open.

"Extra expense" must be "necessary to avoid or mitigate" interruption and incurred "to actually minimize" foregone business income, with no measure for either requirement. Whether spending that failed to reduce lost income qualifies is unresolved.

"Period of interruption" fixes only when the period commences and never states when it ends, so the definition standing alone gives the loss period no outer limit. The measure of "necessarily suspended" is also unstated.

"Rental income" is keyed to a "suspension" of a rented covered location, while the coverage grant and "business income" are keyed to a "period of interruption" and "business interruption" — different defined triggers. Which trigger measures lost rent is unresolved between the definitions.

"Suspension" turns on the premises being "rendered untenantable for the purposes identified to the Insurer at the inception of the Policy", purposes that appear nowhere in the Policy documents. Both "untenantable" and the unrecorded purposes are indeterminate.

The period of interruption begins "on the date the operations would have begun" but for the condition, a wholly hypothetical date with no method of proof or benchmark. When a delayed start-up period begins is therefore open.

The second sentence withholds coverage for lost business income "as a result of unfavorable business conditions caused by the impact of the 'covered pollution condition'", which is difficult to distinguish from the market-driven loss the coverage otherwise insures. The line between covered interruption loss and excluded "unfavorable business conditions" is not drawn.

The appraisal clause is internally garbled — "A decision agreed to by the appraisers, of the umpire, if necessary, shall be binding" — and then requires each party to "[b]ear the other expenses of the appraisal and umpire equally". Whether an umpire's decision alone binds, and who pays what, cannot be read off the text.

The Insurer's retention of "all of its rights pursuant to the Policy to deny all or a portion of the claim" cannot readily be squared with Condition IV.C.'s statement that the appraisers' or umpire's decision "shall be binding upon both parties". What an appraisal actually decides is left in doubt.

The added exclusion bars business interruption loss related to "any of the individually excluded exposures identified above", but nothing "above" in this endorsement identifies excluded exposures. The phrase has no antecedent, leaving the exclusion's content to be supplied by argument.

The grant is for costs "in excess of the 'self-insured retention'", a term Definition V.AA. ties to Items 2.d. and 3.d., while this endorsement separately states a Catastrophe Management-Specific Self-Insured Retention of $100,000. Which retention must be exhausted, and whether both apply to one event, is unresolved.

The trigger is keyed to events commencing "on or after the inception date identified in Item 2.a." rather than during the "policy period" used everywhere else, and Item 2.a. governs Coverage A only. For a Coverage B condition the timing benchmark this clause supplies does not match the coverage it sits on.

The Aggregate Sublimit is made "subject to the Limits of Liability identified in the Declarations", yet those limits are expressed in Section II. as caps on claims, remediation costs and legal defense expense, not on "catastrophe management costs". Whether such costs erode Items 2.–4. is not answered here.

This replacement gives the insured "the right and the duty" to retain a consultant or catastrophe management firm, while the same endorsement's replacement of VII.C. forbids any insured from retaining one without the Insurer's prior written consent. The duty and the prohibition cannot both be performed if consent is refused.

"Adverse media coverage" requires "national or regional news exposure" that is "reasonably likely to have a negative impact" on income, reputation, community relations, public confidence or good will, none of which is measurable. Both the geographic threshold and the likelihood of harm are undefined.

The trigger depends on "the good faith opinion of a 'key executive'" that claims will exceed the retention and that services are needed, making the insured's own subjective view the coverage condition. Whether the Insurer can contest that opinion is not stated.

Item 2. is garbled ("printing, advertising, mailing of materials of public relations materials") and item 5. ends in an open catch-all — "or other necessary response costs" — after a list of medical, funeral, counseling, travel and temporary living costs. The reach of the catch-all against the enumerated specifics is the tension.

This replacement forbids any insured from retaining a consultant or catastrophe management firm without prior written consent, while the same endorsement's replacement of III.C. imposes on the insured "the right and the duty" to retain one. The two provisions of one endorsement pull in opposite directions.

The added exclusion bars catastrophe management costs related to "any of the individually excluded exposures identified above", but nothing above in this endorsement identifies any excluded exposure. The reference has no antecedent.

Every Retroactive Date in the schedule is the policy inception date (and two are typed "11/01/2074" and "41/01/2014"), which leaves nothing for paragraph 2. of the replacement Coverage A timing clause — coverage for conditions commencing before the policy period — to operate on. Whether the Retroactive-Date locations obtained any pre-inception coverage turns on that.

This replacement of Insuring Agreement I.A. is itself deleted "in its entirety" by Endorsement 10, which substitutes a version without any retroactive-date paragraph. Which text grants Coverage A at the Retroactive-Date locations is a direct conflict.

This timing clause extends Coverage A to conditions commencing before the policy period but on or after a Retroactive Date, whereas Endorsement 10's later replacement of I.A. limits Coverage A to conditions commencing entirely during the policy period. The two cannot both fix the timing of Coverage A.

"All other terms and conditions of this Policy remain unchanged" cannot be squared with Endorsement 10's deletion and replacement of the very insuring agreement this endorsement re-wrote. The boilerplate does not tell a reader which endorsement survives.

The replacement per-condition limit is expressed only for "claims" and "remediation costs", dropping "legal defense expense" that the deleted text included, while III.D. as replaced still makes defense expense erode limits. Whether Item 2.b. caps defense expense is left unclear by the omission.

This subsection makes the Item 2.c. aggregate ($9,000,000) the maximum liability, which exceeds the Item 4. Total Policy Aggregate ($7,000,000) that II.G. makes the ceiling. The two aggregates cannot both be maxima.

The Coverage B per-condition limit is confined to conditions "resulting from 'covered operations'", a quoted term that appears nowhere in Section V. or in any endorsement's definitions. The limitation has no defined content.

The Coverage B aggregate is likewise confined to conditions "resulting from 'covered operations'", a quoted term the Policy never defines. Whether the aggregate applies to all Coverage B conditions or only some cannot be told from the words used.

The duty to defend is said to end on exhaustion of the Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit, while Subsection F. added by the same endorsement has the Insurer retain a right to defend after that exhaustion and the following paragraph contemplates continued defense at the Insurer's expense eroding Item 4. Whether defense continues after the sublimit is exhausted is unresolved between them.

Defense expense is made to reduce both the Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit and the Item 4. aggregate and also to be "applied to the 'self-insured retention'", which cannot be squared with II.A.'s statement that "[u]nder no circumstances shall the Insurer be liable to pay any amount within the 'self-insured retention'". Whether the Insurer funds defense within the retention and double-erodes the limits is a direct conflict.

The $2,000,000 dedicated defense sublimit is made subject only to the Item 4. Total Policy Aggregate, while III.D. as replaced has defense expense also reduce that aggregate and be applied to the retention. How the sublimit interacts with the per-condition limits in Items 2.b. and 3.b. (also $2,000,000) is not stated.

The Insurer's retained "right, but not the duty" to defend after exhaustion sits against Subsection A. of the same endorsement, which ends the duty, and against the following paragraph giving the first named insured the right to select counsel subject to Insurer consent. Who controls the defense after exhaustion depends on reconciling the three.

The settlement sentence is garbled — "If the insurer recommends a settlement of any ongoing or future 'claim' for which it is not which is acceptable to a claimant" — so the condition on which the Insurer's liability is capped cannot be read. The mechanical defect changes, and may destroy, the operation of the cap.

The paragraph caps the Insurer's "liability for covered 'loss'", using a quoted term that this Policy never defines, whereas the rest of the instrument speaks of "claims", "remediation costs" and "legal defense expense". What the cap applies to is undefined.

This paragraph makes post-exhaustion defense expense reduce the Item 4. aggregate, which Subsection D. of the same endorsement already provides for all legal defense expense. Whether defense expense erodes Item 4. once or twice is left unresolved between them.

This ninety-day basic extended reporting period replaces Section VIII.C.'s sixty days, but both texts remain printed in the instrument. Which period the first named insured actually has is a direct conflict.
